report.tagline: A US grocery delivery app where personal shoppers pick your order from stores like Costco, Kroger and Safeway and bring it to your door.
report.simpleSummary: Instacart does not own any stores or warehouses. You pick a store you already like in the app, add items, and a shopper walks that store, fills your cart and drives it to you, often within an hour or two. Instacart earns from your fees, from the stores that partner with it, and more and more from brands that pay for ads inside the app. In October 2026 DoorDash agreed to buy it for about $17 billion.

overview.whatItDoes: Instacart is a grocery marketplace that partners with existing retailers instead of owning inventory. Founded in 2012 by Apoorva Mehta and listed on Nasdaq in 2023 as Maplebear (CART), it is run by CEO Chris Rogers. Besides the consumer app, it sells technology to grocers: online store software, smart shopping carts and an ad platform.
howItWorks: You choose a store near you, browse its items and prices in the app, and pay Instacart.
A gig shopper gets the order, shops it in the store, messages you about replacements, pays with an Instacart card, and delivers.
Some retailers pick orders with their own staff and use Instacart only for delivery or software.
Brands like PepsiCo or General Mills buy sponsored spots in search and on shelves inside the app.
Instacart+ members pay a yearly or monthly fee for $0 delivery on larger orders.
Retailers can also license Instacart's tech (Storefront Pro, Caper Carts, Carrot Ads) for their own websites and stores.
overview.valueProposition: For shoppers: your usual store, delivered, without the trip. For retailers: online sales and delivery without building it themselves. For brands: ads at the moment people are deciding what to buy.

painPoints.pain: Grocery shopping takes hours each week
painPoints.howSolved: Shoppers do the shopping and deliver in as little as an hour.

painPoints.pain: Wanting your own store and brands, not a warehouse's limited range
painPoints.howSolved: Shop from about 100,000 real stores, including Costco, Kroger, Publix and Aldi.

painPoints.pain: Small grocers cannot build online shopping
painPoints.howSolved: Instacart gives them app listings, websites and delivery as a service.

painPoints.pain: Brands want to reach shoppers at the point of purchase
painPoints.howSolved: Sponsored product ads inside the app and on retailer sites.

painPoints.pain: Low-income families need delivery with food benefits
painPoints.howSolved: Many stores accept EBT SNAP payments through Instacart.

coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Huge choice without owning any stock or stores.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Shoppers suggest replacements and customers approve in real time.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Out-of-stock items are the biggest quality problem in grocery delivery.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: $99 a year or $9.99 a month for $0 delivery on orders over $35 and lower service fees.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Members order more often and stay longer.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Brands pay for sponsored placements; retailers can run Instacart's ad tech on their own sites.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: About 30% of revenue and high margin; the main reason Instacart is profitable.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Smart shopping carts that scan items in-store, and white-label online store software.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Makes Instacart a tech partner to grocers, not only a delivery app.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Priority delivery in about 30 minutes in some areas, or scheduled windows and store pickup.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Competes with DoorDash and Uber on speed.

businessModel.summary: Instacart takes a cut of each order through customer fees and retailer fees, and earns ad money from brands. It does not own stock, so it avoids warehouse costs but pays shoppers for each order.

revenueStreams.detail: Delivery fees, service fees, Instacart+ fees and retailer fees; $764 million in Q3 2026.
Sponsored ads from brands and enterprise software; $331 million in Q3 2026.
Storefront Pro, Caper Carts and Carrot Ads licensed to retailers.

businessModel.pricing: Delivery fees start around $3.99 for non-members on orders over $35; service fees are a percentage of the order; tips are extra. Instacart+ costs $99 a year or $9.99 a month. Item prices can be higher than in store depending on the retailer.
costDrivers: Shopper pay for picking and delivering
Refunds and credits for missing or damaged items
Engineering for apps, ads and retailer tools
businessModel.unitEconomics: On an average order of about $115, Instacart's revenue is about $12: about $8.35 from fees and retailer cuts and about $3.60 from ads. The biggest cost is paying the shopper, but the ad money has very little cost. Adjusted EBITDA was $342 million on 91.4 million orders in Q3 2026, roughly $3.70 profit per order before some costs. Without ads, it would earn much less on each order.

howTheyGetUsers: Partnerships with big chains like Costco and Kroger that send customers to Instacart
Instacart+ trials and bundles with partners like Chase
SNAP/EBT support bringing low-income families online
whatBringsUsersBack: Weekly grocery habit with 'Buy it again'
growth.moat: Instacart has integrated with 2,200+ retail banners: their catalogues, prices and stock. That took a decade. It also has years of data on what people buy, which powers its ad business. Rivals can add grocery delivery, but rebuilding retailer trust and data is slow.

competitors.name: DoorDash
competitors.positioning: Largest US food delivery app, adding grocery; agreed to buy Instacart in 2026.

competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Instacart has more grocery partners and better shopper tools for big baskets.

northStar.metric: Grocery orders delivered complete and on time per week
northStar.why: A complete, on-time order means the customer saved time and got what they wanted, the retailer made a sale, and the shopper earned. It drives repeat orders and ad value.

pmLessons: You can build a big business without owning inventory by partnering with those who do.
Ads can be a major revenue stream for a marketplace; Instacart's ad revenue is about 30% of the total and very profitable.
Partners can become rivals. Retailers want Instacart's help, but also want to own their customers.
Grocery quality is about the details: found rate and good replacements matter more than delivery speed.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you grow Instacart's ad revenue without hurting user experience?
interviewQuestions.hint: Separate users, brands and retailers. Ideas: better targeting, ad caps, measuring relevance. Guardrail: search-to-cart rate.

interviewQuestions.question: Why would a grocer partner with Instacart instead of building its own delivery?
interviewQuestions.hint: Cost, time, tech, shopper supply, demand. Then the risks: data and customer ownership. Suggest how Instacart reduces those risks.

interviewQuestions.question: How should Instacart and DoorDash combine after the deal?
interviewQuestions.hint: Customers, shoppers/Dashers, retailers and ads. One app or two? Key risk: losing retailers. Metrics: grocery orders and retailer retention.

interviewQuestions.question: Found rate dropped 3 points. What do you do?
interviewQuestions.hint: Segment by retailer, store, category and time. Check stock data accuracy and shopper behaviour. Fix the biggest cause.

interviewQuestions.question: Pick a north star metric for Instacart.
interviewQuestions.hint: Complete, on-time orders per week. Break into active customers, frequency, quality and ad value.

glossary.meaning: A platform that connects buyers and sellers and earns a cut of each sale.
Stock of goods a company owns and holds to sell.
Gross transaction value: the total value of all goods ordered on the platform.
Short, flexible jobs paid per task, like one grocery order.
Software one company builds that another company uses under its own brand.
Earnings before interest, tax and accounting charges for wear of assets; a rough measure of operating profit.
Laws that stop companies from becoming too dominant through mergers or unfair practices.
The share of ordered items that the shopper actually finds in the store.
The share of customers or partners who stop using a product in a period.
Something that makes a business hard for rivals to copy.
The one number a team watches to know if users are getting real value.
